title: MEGOBARI Act
summary: This bill responds to democratic backsliding in the nation of Georgia and its government's deepening ties with Russia, China, and Iran. It directs reports and a five-year U.S. strategy on Georgia, and sets up sanctions — visa bans and asset freezes — against Georgian officials and others who engage in corruption or violence to block Georgia's integration with Europe and NATO or who undermine Georgia's sovereignty. It also offers a path to expanded U.S. cooperation if Georgia's government demonstrates democratic progress. The whole Act sunsets after five years.
brief: Authorizes visa and financial sanctions on Georgian officials who block Euro-Atlantic integration or undermine Georgia's sovereignty, and orders reports and a five-year U.S. strategy on Georgia.

top_lines.headline: Sanctions on Georgian Officials
subs: President must determine within 90 days which Georgian officials blocked Euro-Atlantic integration through corruption or violence
Mandatory visa ineligibility and revocation for those affirmatively identified
Discretionary asset freezes plus mandatory visa sanctions for undermining Georgia's sovereignty

top_lines.headline: Reports and Strategy
subs: Classified report on Russian intelligence assets in Georgia within 180 days, with a China annex
Five-year U.S. bilateral strategy within 90 days, including whether Georgia stays the second-highest U.S. funding recipient in Europe and Eurasia

top_lines.headline: Conditional Re-engagement
subs: If the President certifies sustained democratic progress, the U.S. should expand exchanges and military cooperation
Sense of Congress to suspend the U.S.-Georgia Strategic Partnership Commission until reforms occur
Entire Act sunsets five years after enactment

likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Wilson (R-SC) with a bipartisan group of cosponsors (Cohen, Hudson, Veasey) and 18 cosponsors total, the bill passed the House and was placed on the Senate calendar. Georgia-focused, anti-Russia sanctions legislation generally draws bipartisan support, but mandatory sanctions on a partner government's officials and the discretionary waiver structure can slow Senate floor consideration.

items.main: Names the Act the “Mobilizing and Enhancing Georgia’s Options for Building Accountability, Resilience, and Independence Act” (the “MEGOBARI Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines key terms used throughout the Act: “appropriate congressional committees,” “NATO,” and “Secretary.”
items.detail: “Appropriate congressional committees” means the Senate and House Committees on Foreign Relations/Foreign Affairs and on Appropriations; “NATO” means the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; “Secretary” means the Secretary of State.

items.main: States the sense of Congress applauding Georgia's post-Soviet progress, noting significant democratic backsliding and the government's growing ties with Russia and China, and urging suspension of the U.S.-Georgia Strategic Partnership Commission until Georgia represents its citizens' democratic wishes and advances EU/NATO membership.
items.detail: Sense-of-Congress section — expresses Congress's view; no binding legal effect. References the U.S.-Georgia Charter on Strategic Partnership of January 9, 2009.

items.main: Declares it U.S. policy to support Georgia's constitutional aspirations to join the EU and NATO, protect its sovereignty from Russian aggression, support democratic development and civil society, and impose consequences on individuals undermining democratic standards.
items.detail: Cites Article 78 of the Constitution of Georgia and the European Commission reform plan; calls for release of persons detained on politically motivated grounds and investigation of the October 2024 national elections.

items.main: Requires a classified report on Russian intelligence penetration in Georgia and a five-year U.S. strategy for bilateral relations.
items.detail: Within 180 days, the Secretary of State, with the Director of National Intelligence and Secretary of Defense, must submit a classified report on Russian intelligence elements and assets in Georgia, with an annex on Chinese influence and potential Russian-Chinese cooperation. Within 90 days, the Secretary and USAID Administrator must submit a five-year strategy outlining objectives for bilateral ties, the tools and funding to achieve them, an assessment of whether Georgia should remain the second-highest recipient of U.S. funding in the Europe and Eurasia region, and a plan to support civil society and independent media. The strategy is unclassified with a classified annex.

items.main: Directs the President to determine within 90 days which Georgian officials and family members knowingly engaged in corruption or violence to block Euro-Atlantic integration, and to impose visa sanctions on them.
items.detail: Covered persons include anyone who served as a Member of Georgia's Parliament or senior party official on or after January 1, 2014, leadership officials of the Georgian government (law enforcement, intelligence, judicial, local), and benefiting immediate family. Those affirmatively identified face mandatory visa ineligibility and revocation under subsection (d)(2). A separate authority lets the President impose IEEPA asset-blocking (discretionary) and visa sanctions (mandatory) on foreign persons who undermine the peace, security, stability, sovereignty, or territorial integrity of Georgia.

items.main: Sets out the sanctions, waivers, exceptions, and a broader-corruption review.
items.detail: Sanctions consist of IEEPA property blocking and visa ineligibility/revocation. The President may waive sanctions for national-security reasons or changed circumstances (renewable 180-day waivers for the sovereignty-based sanctions). Implementing regulations are due within 120 days. Within 180 days the President must report on foreign persons engaged in significant corruption in Georgia. Exceptions cover authorized intelligence activities, U.N. headquarters obligations, humanitarian and agricultural/medical transactions, and the importation of goods. Sanctions terminate when the President certifies a person has stopped the triggering conduct or at the Act's sunset.

sections.label: Section 7 — Additional Assistance With Respect to Georgia

items.main: Provides for expanded U.S. cooperation with Georgia if the President certifies sustained democratic progress.
items.detail: Upon the President's certification that Georgia has shown significant and sustained progress reinvigorating its democracy and advancing Euro-Atlantic integration, the Secretary of State should enhance people-to-people contacts and academic exchanges, and the President, with the Secretary of Defense, should maintain and as appropriate expand military cooperation — including territorial-defense equipment and related training — to help deter Russian aggression.

items.main: Provides that the Act ceases to have any force or effect beginning on the date that is 5 years after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Sunset provision — terminates the Act's authorities five years after enactment.

underreported.summary: The mandatory inadmissibility review reaches any individual who served as a Member of Georgia's Parliament or as a senior official of a Georgian political party at any point on or after January 1, 2014, not only current officeholders.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around responding to recent backsliding, but this provision applies the corruption/violence screen to more than a decade of past and former parliamentarians and party officials, a far wider pool than sitting government officials.

underreported.summary: The required five-year strategy must include an assessment of whether Georgia should remain the second-highest recipient of U.S. funding in the Europe and Eurasia region.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond the sanctions headline, this directs an explicit review that could lead to reducing Georgia's U.S. assistance, a budgetary consequence not evident from the bill's title.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Wilson
featured_quotes.text: Madam Speaker, I am grateful for the bipartisan endorsement of this legislation. It is bipartisan with Republican and Democratic support and bicameral with Senate and House support of the MEGOBARI bill, which promotes the brave people of the Republic of Georgia. For more than 155 days, the freedom-loving people of Georgia have peacefully taken to the streets in defense of the future and soul of their nation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Davidson
featured_quotes.text: Madam Speaker, I generally support everything that the chairman supports. This is a wrongheaded bill. Our colleagues need to say ``no'' to this. The American people did not send us here to expand America's security blanket to more parts of the world. We don't have to get involved in every conflict we are invited to, and we certainly don't need to seek out extra ones. We can wish the people of Georgia well without expanding our commitment to be Europe's defense force with a blank check to defend every country.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cohen
featured_quotes.text: Madam Speaker, Georgia has long been a great friend to the United States. I went to Georgia for their election when they elected the Georgian Dream ticket about 12 years ago, but the Georgian Dream party has turned into the Georgian nightmare. In America, Dr. King had a dream, and that dream still lives. Yet, the dream in Georgia, the country, is no longer alive and is pulling that country closer to our adversaries.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Olszewski
featured_quotes.text: H.R. 36 works to show the people of Georgia that the  United States remains committed to its Euro-Atlantic aspirations and provides a framework for appropriate cooperation with the Georgian Government in light of worrying democratic backsliding in the country.

gaps: The bill mandates a determination of which officials blocked Euro-Atlantic integration but does not define the threshold of 'significant acts of corruption' that triggers mandatory sanctions.
The bill directs an assessment of whether Georgia should remain the second-highest U.S. funding recipient but does not itself change or condition any specific assistance program.
The bill provides broad national-security waivers for sanctions but does not set a limit on how many covered officials may be waived or for how long in aggregate.
The bill sets a five-year sunset for the entire Act but does not address what happens to sanctions still in effect on persons who continue the triggering conduct after sunset.

added: Mandatory visa sanctions on Georgian officials and family members determined to have engaged in corruption or violence blocking Euro-Atlantic integration
Discretionary IEEPA asset-blocking and mandatory visa sanctions for foreign persons undermining Georgia's sovereignty or territorial integrity
A classified report on Russian intelligence assets in Georgia and a five-year U.S. bilateral strategy
A five-year sunset on the entire Act
